record.description: Dimensionless ratio comparing a particle species’ kinetic temperature with the positive reference temperature on the same magnetic flux surface.
record.documentation:
The quantity expresses the kinetic temperature of a selected particle species relative to a single reference thermal scale on the same magnetic flux surface. It is the normalized counterpart of [particle temperature](name:particle_temperature), while retaining the species dependence of the numerator.

It is defined by

$$
T_p^{\mathrm{norm}} = \frac{T_p}{T_{\mathrm{ref}}}
$$

where $T_p$ is the kinetic temperature of the selected particle species and $T_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the positive reference temperature for the flux surface.

The ratio is dimensionless and is not an absolute temperature; its value depends on the specified reference temperature.
record.name: ratio_of_particle_temperature_to_particle_reference_temperature

reason: The definition omits the emission-band application and its shared-channel convention: "Lower bound of the energy band" within "Emissivity profile per energy band (assumed common to all channels used in the profile reconstruction)". It also omits the stated dimensions and unit: "unit=eV ndim=2" for "Lower energy detection threshold on each pixel of the detector", versus "unit=eV ndim=0" for the channel and emissivity-profile bounds.

record.description: Lower-bound photon energy sets the low-energy cutoff for X-ray photon counting, admitting only photons above the threshold of the specified detector pixel or channel. For an energy-resolved emission band, the bound instead specifies the low-energy boundary of the included emission and is assumed common to all channels used in the profile reconstruction. Values are expressed in eV, stored as a two-dimensional per-pixel array for the X-ray camera and as a scalar for each detector-channel energy band or emissivity-profile energy band.
record.documentation:
Lower-bound photon energy is the low-energy edge of an X-ray detection or emission band. For photon counting, it is the threshold that an incident photon must exceed to be eligible for registration.

The lower-threshold requirement for counting is:

$$
E_{\gamma} > E_{\gamma,\min}
$$

where $E_{\gamma}$ is the incident photon energy and $E_{\gamma,\min}$ is the lower photon-energy threshold assigned to the specified detector pixel or channel.

The counting threshold applies individually to that pixel or channel, rather than representing an average over the detector. For an energy-resolved emission band, the bound instead specifies the low-energy boundary of the included emission.

Together with [upper photon energy](name:upper_photon_energy), this bound specifies the spectral window. It is a band boundary, not a [central or representative pixel photon energy](name:energy_of_detector_pixel). Exceeding the lower threshold is necessary for counting but does not imply unit detection probability.
record.name: lower_bound_photon_energy

reason: The source specifies "Number of effective turns in the element for calculating magnetic fields of the coil/loop" and "positive means current is counter-clockwise when seen from above". Its enclosure states "Each loop is comprised of a number of cross-section elements described individually" and describes "axisymmetric conducting elements not actively driven by a power supply". These require the element locus and the explicit magnetic-field purpose and sign convention.

record.description: Effective turn count of a passive loop element is the signed number of equivalent windings assigned to a passive axisymmetric conducting loop element for electromagnetic coupling in calculating magnetic fields of the coil/loop. It weights the passive-loop current contribution and may be fractional for equivalent or homogenized loop elements. Positive means current is counter-clockwise when seen from above. It is a dimensionless scalar with unit 1.
record.documentation:
Effective turn count of a passive loop element is the signed number of equivalent windings assigned to a passive conducting loop element for electromagnetic coupling. It may be fractional when the represented conductor is an equivalent or homogenized passive-loop element rather than a literal winding. Positive means current is counter-clockwise when seen from above.

The signed current-turn source strength represented by the passive loop element is defined by:

$$
\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{loop}} = N_{\mathrm{eff}} I_{\mathrm{loop}}
$$

where $\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{loop}}$ is the signed current-turn source strength of the passive loop element, $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the effective turn count of the passive loop element, and $I_{\mathrm{loop}}$ is the [current of the passive loop](name:current_of_passive_loop).

This quantity applies to the represented passive-loop element as one electromagnetic circuit contribution. Each loop is comprised of a number of cross-section elements described individually. It has no implicit aggregation over multiple passive loops; if several represented windings or conductor pieces are collapsed into one loop element, their net orientation and coupling are represented by the single algebraic value of $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$.

It is distinct from the [current of the passive loop](name:current_of_passive_loop), which is multiplied by $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$, and from the [area of the passive loop](name:area_of_passive_loop), which describes conductor cross section. It is not a turn count for magnetic probes, coil conductor elements, toroidal-field coils, or magnetic field-line winding.
record.name: effective_turn_count_of_passive_loop_element

reason: The incumbent specifies "Polarization angle of motional Stark effect emission at a constraint position", requiring the identifying motional_stark qualifier. The resulting name, "motional_stark_polarization_angle_at_constraint_position", already appears among the neighbours with the definition "Polarization angle of Stark-split Balmer-alpha light from neutral-beam atoms at a constraint position specifies its linear-polarization orientation for the selected viewing geometry." The case file supplies no physical distinction permitting a separate name.

record.description: Polarization angle of motional Stark effect emission at a constraint position: the angular orientation of the linear-polarization axis of the beam emission for the specified neutral-beam and viewing geometry, whether realized as an observed angle or as the angle consistent with a reconstructed equilibrium state.
record.documentation:
Polarization angle of motional Stark effect emission at a constraint position is the angular orientation of the linear-polarization axis of the light emitted by injected neutral-beam atoms, for the specified neutral-beam and viewing geometry.

The polarization angle is defined by

$$
\alpha = \operatorname{atan2}\!\left(\hat{\mathbf p}\cdot\hat{\mathbf e}_2,\;\hat{\mathbf p}\cdot\hat{\mathbf e}_1\right) \pmod{\pi}
$$

where $\alpha$ is the polarization angle, $\hat{\mathbf p}$ is a unit vector along the linear-polarization axis of the emission, and $\hat{\mathbf e}_1$ and $\hat{\mathbf e}_2$ are orthonormal unit vectors spanning the viewing plane perpendicular to the line of sight: $\hat{\mathbf e}_1$ sets the angular zero and $\hat{\mathbf e}_2$ sets the positive angular direction. Reduction modulo a half-turn reflects that linear polarization defines an axis rather than an oriented vector, so orientations differing by a half-turn are equivalent.

The quantity is specific to the constraint position and to the stated beam and viewing geometry; it is not an average over positions, beams, or sightlines. It may denote the observed emission polarization orientation or the orientation that a reconstructed equilibrium state implies for the same geometry; both realizations denote the same physical angle.

It is not a residual between observed and equilibrium-consistent values, not a statistical weight, and not the magnetic-field pitch angle: the correspondence between this angle and the local magnetic-field pitch depends on the beam velocity, the viewing geometry, and the selected Stark polarization component. It is a geometry-specific form of the polarization angle, and it differs from the [Faraday angle](name:faraday_angle), which is a propagation-induced rotation of polarization rather than an emission polarization orientation.

Sign convention: Positive when the polarization axis rotates from the zero-angle reference direction $\hat{\mathbf e}_1$ toward the positive reference direction $\hat{\mathbf e}_2$ within the viewing plane.
record.name: polarization_angle_at_constraint_position

reason: The source specifies “Normalised collisionality between two species”, and the recorded source qualification is normalization to “a characteristic transit frequency”, not the incumbent's “streaming, transit, or bounce frequency”. The bound source also states “ndim=2”, which must appear in the definition.

record.description: Dimensionless ratio of a specified interspecies collision frequency to the characteristic transit frequency used for the plasma population. It is represented as a two-dimensional array indexed by the two particle species and has unit 1.
record.documentation:
This collisionality measures the strength of interspecies collisional relaxation relative to collisionless motion along magnetic-field trajectories.

$$
\nu_{ab}^{*} = \frac{\nu_{ab}}{\omega_{\mathrm{char}}}
$$

where $\nu_{ab}$ is the collision frequency between species $a$ and $b$, and $\omega_{\mathrm{char}}$ is the relevant characteristic transit frequency; both quantities have reciprocal-time units.

The denominator must be interpreted as the characteristic transit frequency for the selected plasma population, so this quantity is distinct from the collision frequency itself. It generalizes the population-specific electron collisionality and complements collisionality at the pedestal top when the characteristic frequency is evaluated there.
record.name: normalized_interspecies_collisionality

record.description: Thermodynamic temperature associated with a selected thermocouple sensor attached to a tokamak structural component.
record.documentation:
This quantity is the absolute thermodynamic temperature associated with one selected sensor member, represented by the thermal state at its thermocouple junction. It characterizes the local thermal condition of the attached structural component at the sensor location.

For a system in thermodynamic equilibrium, temperature is defined by

$$
T = \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial S}\right)_{V,N}
$$

where $T$ is thermodynamic temperature, $U$ is internal energy, $S$ is entropy, $V$ is volume, and $N$ is the amount of material or particle number held fixed in the derivative.

The quantity applies to the selected sensor member individually and is not a sum, average, or other aggregation over the sensor set. It denotes the sensor or junction thermal state associated with a structural component, not the temperature of a flowing coolant or of an entire plant connection.

It is distinct from [coolant temperature at inlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_inlet), which describes fluid entering a cooling system. Object-specific quantities such as [temperature of a coil conductor](name:temperature_of_coil_conductor) and [temperature of a neutron detector](name:temperature_of_neutron_detector) apply the same thermodynamic concept to explicitly named hardware rather than to the generic sensor locus.
record.name: temperature_of_sensor

reason: The case states, "The coordinate's scale is essential to the definition," but supplies "none (no DD source is bound to this target)" and reports "Missing: bound_source". The incumbent's unit "1" requires a length-valued coordinate for the stated physical-space gradient, whereas its documentation also discusses a "dimensionless normalized flux radius" without establishing the coordinate actually used. The neighbouring record's reference to a "length-valued toroidal-flux coordinate" does not establish this target's coordinate convention. The case therefore cannot determine whether to specify a length-valued coordinate or correct the unit to inverse-square length.

The definition omits numerical details specified by “Normalised toroidal beta, defined as 100 * beta_tor * a[m] * B0 [T] / ip [MA]”, the pressure method specified by “using the pressure determined by an equilibrium reconstruction code”, and the averaging and pressure component identified by “volume-averaged total perpendicular plasma pressure”. The enclosing structures specify “0D parameters of the equilibrium” and “Set of equilibria at various time slices”; the profile-derived and summary sources specify “ndim=1”. These details must be explicit in the definition.

record.description:
Normalized toroidal beta is the whole-plasma toroidal pressure beta rescaled by minor radius and signed reference toroidal field relative to plasma current. It is dimensionless (unit 1), with defining normalization beta_N = 100 * beta_tor * a[m] * B0[T] / Ip[MA], where a is the positive plasma minor radius, B0 is the nonzero signed reference vacuum toroidal magnetic field and Ip is the nonzero signed net toroidal plasma current; their numerical values are taken in metres, teslas and megaamperes, respectively. The underlying beta_tor = 2*mu_0*

/B0^2 uses vacuum permeability mu_0 and the whole-plasma volume average

of total perpendicular plasma pressure, including the represented thermal and nonthermal contributions. For the equilibrium-reconstruction variant, the pressure is determined by an equilibrium reconstruction code without changing the normalization. The signed ratio B0/Ip is preserved. The quantity is a global scalar evaluated at each equilibrium time slice; the bound profile-derived and summary representations are one-dimensional arrays.
record.documentation:
Normalized toroidal beta is the conventional current-and-geometry rescaling of the whole-plasma toroidal pressure beta. Its defining normalization is $\beta_{\mathrm{N}}=100\,\beta_{\mathrm{tor}}\,a[\mathrm{m}]\,B_0[\mathrm{T}]/I_p[\mathrm{MA}]$. Here $\beta_{\mathrm{N}}$ is normalized toroidal beta, $\beta_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the dimensionless [toroidal beta](name:toroidal_beta), $a$ is plasma minor radius, $B_0$ is the signed reference vacuum toroidal magnetic field and $I_p$ is the signed net toroidal plasma current. The bracketed units specify the numerical values used in this conventional normalization.

The underlying toroidal pressure ratio, before that rescaling, obeys $$\beta = \frac{2\mu_0 \langle p\rangle}{B^2}$$ with $\beta=\beta_{\mathrm{tor}}$, $B=B_0$, $\mu_0$ vacuum permeability and $\langle p\rangle$ the whole-plasma volume average of the total perpendicular pressure $p$ used to form the toroidal beta. This pressure-ratio equation defines the operand $\beta_{\mathrm{tor}}$; it is not the defining equation of $\beta_{\mathrm{N}}$.

The pressure input includes the thermal and nonthermal contributions represented by the total-pressure input. A pressure estimate obtained from equilibrium reconstruction changes that pressure input rather than the normalization. Restricting the pressure input to thermal pressure defines the separately named [normalized toroidal thermal beta](name:normalized_toroidal_thermal_beta).

The normalization requires positive minor radius and nonzero reference field and plasma current. It preserves the signed ratio $B_0/I_p$ without silently replacing either by its magnitude. For nonnegative underlying toroidal beta, the sign of the normalized value follows that ratio. The normalized quantity differs from unnormalized toroidal beta by the explicit factor of 100 and the stated size, field and current factors.
record.name: normalized_toroidal_beta

reason: The limiter registry states: “At the limiter, a measurement refers to the scrape-off-layer plasma immediately adjacent to its surface; the precise plasma evaluation point is not specified.” This contradicts the incumbent's specified magnetic-presheath or sheath-entrance evaluation point. The bound source specifies “unit=m^-3”.

record.description: Local particle number density of hydrogen ions in the boundary plasma immediately adjacent to a plasma-facing limiter surface; the precise plasma evaluation point is not specified. The unit is m^-3.
record.documentation:
Hydrogen density at a limiter is the local number density of hydrogen ions in the boundary plasma immediately adjacent to a plasma-facing limiter surface. The precise plasma evaluation point is not specified; neutral hydrogen is excluded. For hydrogen, the charge-state sum reduces to the density of positively charged hydrogen ions, H+.

The local hydrogen-ion density is defined from the velocity distribution function:

$$
n_{\mathrm{H}^+} = \int f_{\mathrm{H}^+}(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{H}^+}$ is the hydrogen-ion number density, $f_{\mathrm{H}^+}$ is the hydrogen-ion velocity distribution function, and $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity at the evaluation point.

This quantity is the hydrogen-specific component of [density_at_limiter](name:density_at_limiter). It counts hydrogen ions separately from [deuterium_density_at_limiter](name:deuterium_density_at_limiter), and does not include neutral hydrogen or other ion species.
record.name: hydrogen_density_at_limiter

reason: The adjudicator states that “back_surface_neutron_flux” denotes “neutron number flux,” whereas the definition specifies “neutron kinetic-energy transfer” and “not a neutron count flux.” Adding energy to the name identifies the explicitly defined quantity while retaining its correct energy-flux unit: “The stored unit ‘W.m^-2’ fits energy flux.”

record.description: Back-surface neutron energy flux is the local rate of neutron kinetic-energy transfer outward through an object's designated rear surface, per unit actual surface area and time. It is a scalar energy flux, not a neutron count flux, integrated power, or spatial maximum. Its unit is W.m^-2.
record.documentation:
Back-surface neutron energy flux is the local rate at which neutron kinetic energy crosses outward through an object's designated rear surface, per unit actual surface area and time. It is a scalar measure of energy transfer, not a neutron count rate.

The local energy flux is defined by

$$
\Gamma_{n,\mathrm{back}}^{E}(\mathbf r,t) = \frac{\partial^2 E_{n,\mathrm{out}}}{\partial A\,\partial t}(\mathbf r,t)
$$

where $\Gamma_{n,\mathrm{back}}^{E}$ is the back-surface neutron energy flux, $n$ identifies the neutron contributions, $\mathbf r$ is position on the back surface, $t$ is time, $E_{n,\mathrm{out}}$ is the cumulative kinetic energy carried by neutrons crossing outward through the surface, and $A$ is actual surface area.

The quantity applies locally over the object's designated back surface and aggregates the kinetic-energy contributions of outward-crossing neutrons across their energies. It excludes neutron number flux, neutron production within a volume, energy deposited inside material, power integrated over a surface, and a spatial maximum or average over the surface.

Integrating the local flux over a portion of the back surface gives the neutron power crossing outward through that portion. The [maximum of back-surface neutron flux](name:maximum_of_back_surface_neutron_flux) is the greatest local value over the applicable back surface; that maximum is not part of this local quantity.
record.name: back_surface_neutron_energy_flux

record.description: Characteristic timescale of electric-current decrease during a disruption, defined by a specified linear-threshold or exponential decay convention.
record.documentation:
This quantity characterizes electric-current decay during a disruption. It encompasses the total plasma current and the current carried by a specified particle population, without imposing a particular current component or decay convention.

For a linear threshold convention, the extrapolated full-decay time is defined by:

$$
\tau_{\mathrm{lin}}=\frac{t(f_{\mathrm{low}})-t(f_{\mathrm{high}})}{f_{\mathrm{high}}-f_{\mathrm{low}}}
$$

where $\tau_{\mathrm{lin}}$ is the linear decay time, $f_{\mathrm{high}}$ and $f_{\mathrm{low}}$ are the upper and lower fractions of a specified reference current magnitude, and $t(f)$ is the time at which the decaying current magnitude reaches fraction $f$ of that reference.

An exponential convention instead defines an e-folding time through $I(t)=I_0\exp[-(t-t_0)/\tau_{\mathrm{exp}}]$, where $I(t)$ is the selected current magnitude at time $t$, $I_0$ is its value at reference time $t_0$, and $\tau_{\mathrm{exp}}$ is the exponential decay time. A linear threshold time is not generally equal to an exponential e-folding time.

The [plasma-current decay time](name:plasma_decay_time_due_to_disruption) uses the linear construction with upper and lower fractions of 0.8 and 0.2. The [runaway-electron current decay time](name:runaway_electron_decay_time_due_to_disruption) applies to the total toroidal runaway-electron current and permits custom linear, fixed 20–80% linear, or exponential conventions. These specializations characterize different current populations and need not have equal decay times; neither denotes a local current-density decay time or an electron-temperature decay time.
record.name: decay_time_due_to_disruption

record.description: Major-radius coordinate of a reference point in a poloidal-field coil's cross-sectional geometry, measured by perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis.
record.documentation:
Major-radius coordinate of poloidal field coil

This coil-specific instance of the [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate) is defined by

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are the transverse coordinates of the same point in a right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame whose $z$ axis coincides with the toroidal symmetry axis and whose vertical coordinate is $z=Z$.

The coordinate is nonnegative and applies to the specified geometric reference point, which need not coincide with the coil center. It is a point location, not an average over the coil or a cross-sectional radius. Unlike the [radial outline of the poloidal-field coil](name:radial_outline_of_poloidal_field_coil), it does not describe the complete cross-sectional boundary.
record.name: radial_coordinate_of_poloidal_field_coil

reason: The definition omits numerical conventions specified elsewhere in the case file: “The contribution is defined by Faraday's law” with “V_{\mathrm{ext}}(t) = -\frac{d\Phi_{\mathrm{ext}}(t)}{dt}”; “the externally generated poloidal magnetic flux linked by the considered toroidal plasma circuit”; “It excludes resistive voltage drops and other non-inductive contributions”; and “Positive when the induced electromotive force has a positive line integral in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.” The recorded reason also specifies a “global 0-D equilibrium quantity”.

record.description: Electromotive-force contribution to the plasma loop voltage caused by changing externally generated poloidal magnetic flux, including flux linked through active coils and passive conducting structures. This global, zero-dimensional scalar is V_ext(t) = -dΦ_ext(t)/dt, where Φ_ext(t) is the externally generated poloidal magnetic flux linked by the considered toroidal plasma circuit and t is time; its unit is V. It excludes resistive voltage drops and other non-inductive contributions. Positive when the induced electromotive force has a positive line integral in the direction of increasing toroidal angle φ in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
record.documentation:
This quantity is the inductive electromotive-force contribution to the plasma loop voltage produced by time-varying poloidal magnetic flux generated by active coil circuits and magnetically coupled passive conducting structures. It excludes resistive voltage drops and other non-inductive contributions.

The contribution is defined by Faraday's law:

$$
V_{\mathrm{ext}}(t) = -\frac{d\Phi_{\mathrm{ext}}(t)}{dt}
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is the externally generated poloidal magnetic flux linked by the considered toroidal plasma circuit and $t$ is time. It contributes to the total [loop voltage at the plasma boundary](name:loop_voltage_at_plasma_boundary); currents in passive conductors are represented by the linked-flux response of structures such as those described by [current of passive structure](name:current_of_passive_structure).

Sign convention: Positive when the induced electromotive force has a positive line integral in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
record.name: external_loop_voltage

reason: The sources specify “Incident angle of the magnetic field with respect to PFC surface”, not the probe’s own surface, and identify embedded probes as “embedded (in a plasma facing component)”. For reciprocating probes, “The time child node corresponds to the time of maximum penetration of the probe during a given plunge.” The adjudicator identifies the domain as “interpretation of ion saturation current measurements,” not mechanical measurement diagnostics.

For a reciprocating probe, the scalar value is associated with a plunge time slice whose time corresponds to maximum probe penetration.
record.documentation: (none recorded)

reason: The source says "Minimum flow rate of the valve", identifying the valve locus omitted from the incumbent name. The supplied neighbour "gas_flow_of_valve" establishes that locus construction, and the qualifier vocabulary supplies "lower_bound" rather than "minimum". The definition now explicitly includes the documented calculation "Q_g = p_g \frac{dV_g}{dt}" and the source unit "Pa.m^3.s^-1".

record.description: Minimum gas flow is the smallest pressure-volume gas throughput that a gas injection valve can reliably deliver, defining the lower bound of its controllable range. Pressure-volume throughput is p_g dV_g/dt, where p_g is gas pressure at the flow boundary and dV_g/dt is the volumetric flow rate across that boundary; the unit is Pa.m^3.s^-1.
record.documentation:
Minimum gas flow is the lower reliable operating limit of the pressure-volume throughput delivered by a gas injection valve. It identifies the smallest controllable value of the aggregate gas stream throughput, rather than a molecular-species flow or particle-number rate.

The pressure-volume throughput represented by this quantity is defined as

$$
Q_g = p_g \frac{dV_g}{dt}
$$

where $Q_g$ is gas pressure-volume throughput, $p_g$ is gas pressure at the flow boundary, $V_g$ is the volume of gas crossing that boundary, and $t$ is time.

This quantity applies to the aggregate gas stream delivered through an injection system across a defined flow boundary. The stream is not restricted to a particular molecular species or charge state, and this quantity is distinct from mass flow and particle-number rate. Its defining distinction is the lower reliable operating bound, rather than an unrestricted instantaneous throughput.

The gas flow quantity defines the same pressure-volume throughput without imposing a lower-limit condition; minimum gas flow is its lower reliable operating bound. Conversely, [maximum gas flow](name:maximum_gas_flow) is the upper reliable operating bound, so the two quantities delimit the controllable range rather than represent different throughput definitions.
record.name: lower_bound_gas_flow_of_valve

reason: The adjudicator identifies “Radial drift of the pellet deposition location relative to the ablation location,” while the bound source specifies “between the ablation and the final deposition locations, in terms of the normalised toroidal flux coordinate”; this is not a toroidal displacement. The enclosing structures specify “1-D profiles of plasma and pellet along the pellet path” and “The time of this structure corresponds to the full ablation of the pellet inside the plasma.” These require the deposition-relative-to-ablation name and the explicit profile and time-slice qualifications in the definition; the coordinate normalisation remains in the definition.

record.description: Shift of pellet-material deposition relative to its ablation location caused by E×B drift, expressed as a difference in normalized toroidal flux coordinate. The difference is final deposition minus ablation, evaluated for material ablated at each corresponding location in a one-dimensional profile along the pellet path, not integrated along the path. The time slice corresponds to full ablation of the pellet inside the plasma. The unit is 1.
record.documentation:
The pellet deposition displacement describes the shift of ablated pellet material from its ablation location to its final deposition location attributable to E-cross-B drift. It is expressed as a difference in normalized toroidal flux coordinate.

The displacement is defined by deposition minus ablation:

$$
\Delta\rho_{\mathrm{tor},\mathrm{N}} = \rho_{\mathrm{tor},\mathrm{N},\mathrm{dep}} - \rho_{\mathrm{tor},\mathrm{N},\mathrm{abl}}
$$

where $\Delta\rho_{\mathrm{tor},\mathrm{N}}$ is the pellet deposition displacement, and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor},\mathrm{N},\mathrm{dep}}$ and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor},\mathrm{N},\mathrm{abl}}$ are the normalized toroidal flux coordinates at the final deposition and ablation locations, respectively.

Each value concerns material ablated at the corresponding location along the pellet path, not a path-integrated displacement. Only the shift attributed to E-cross-B drift is included. This coordinate difference is neither an absolute deposition coordinate nor a geometric distance or drift velocity; it describes redistribution of ablated material rather than the injection motion characterized by the [initial pellet velocity](name:initial_velocity_of_pellet).
record.name: radial_displacement_of_pellet_deposition_relative_to_ablation_due_to_e_cross_b_drift

reason: The source specifies “Thickness of this layer evaluated at the midplane”; the incumbent name, definition and documentation omit the midplane locus.

record.description: Non-negative geometric separation between the inner and outer material interfaces of a breeder blanket layer along the specified thickness direction, evaluated at the midplane, in m.
record.documentation:
Non-negative geometric separation between the inner and outer material interfaces of a breeder blanket layer is the local through-thickness of that layer along the specified thickness direction, evaluated at the midplane. The quantity applies to a single material or functional layer within the blanket, not to the total breeder blanket module build.

The layer thickness is defined by the separation of the two bounding interfaces along the thickness coordinate:

$$
d_\ell = \left|s_{\ell,\mathrm{out}} - s_{\ell,\mathrm{in}}\right|
$$

where $d_\ell$ is the layer thickness in m, and $s_{\ell,\mathrm{in}}$ and $s_{\ell,\mathrm{out}}$ are the signed coordinates in m of the inner and outer layer interfaces along the specified thickness direction.

It is not the toroidal width, poloidal height, surface extent, or volume-equivalent thickness of the layer. It is distinct from module-level quantities such as thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module, [lower_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:lower_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module), and [upper_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:upper_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module). For a radially stacked layer, the thickness direction is the cylindrical $\hat{R}$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.
record.name: thickness_of_breeder_blanket_layer_at_midplane

reason: The adjudicator states: "The name 'radius_of_poloidal_field_coil' identifies a coil radius, but the definition specifies the 'curvature radius of one arc-of-circle segment used to approximate the cross-sectional contour'—the local radius of a contour segment, not the radius of the coil." The name therefore needs the curvature distinction; the stated unit "m" is also made explicit in the definition.

record.description: Non-negative curvature radius, in m, of one arc-of-circle segment used to approximate the cross-sectional contour of a poloidal field coil. The contour lies in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where R is major radius and Z is vertical height.
record.documentation:
Radius of a poloidal-field-coil arc is the non-negative circle radius of a single circular segment of the coil cross-sectional contour, taken in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. The conductor or winding-pack boundary is approximated by connected circular arcs, and this quantity sets the local radius of curvature of one such arc.

For a circular contour segment, the curvature radius $\rho$ (in m) is the inverse magnitude of the planar curvature $\kappa$ (in m$^{-1}$) of the boundary curve in the $(R, Z)$ cross-section:

$$
\rho = \frac{1}{|\kappa|}
$$

where a finite physical arc has $\rho > 0$, and as $\rho$ grows the segment approaches a straight line ($\kappa \to 0$). Each arc is anchored by a start point in the poloidal plane: its major-radius coordinate is given by major_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil and its vertical coordinate by [height_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:height_of_poloidal_field_coil); both together with $\rho$ are needed to locate and shape one arc, with the end of each arc coinciding with the start of the next.

The value is determined from the designed circular-arc contour, from CAD geometry, or by fitting circular arcs to surveyed boundary points. Small radii represent tightly rounded corners and compact winding-pack features, while larger radii represent gently curved coil sides; the magnitude scales with coil aperture, winding-pack dimensions, and mechanical-clearance requirements. An analogous arc-of-circle convention applies to iron core segment boundaries via radius_of_iron_core_segment.
record.name: curvature_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil

reason: The source specifies “Sign of the toroidal magnetic field” under “Flux surface characteristics”; the recorded adjudication states that the name “omits the magnetic-field identification and flux-surface locus.” The definition also needs the stated convention: “The component is $B_\phi = \mathbf{B}\cdot\hat{\phi}$,” in the “right-handed cylindrical frame,” and the restriction that the indicator is “undefined when the toroidal component vanishes.”

record.description: Orientation indicator equal to the sign of the toroidal magnetic-field component on a flux surface in local gyrokinetic geometry. It is the dimensionless scalar s_phi = B_phi/|B_phi|, where B_phi = B · phi_hat is the equilibrium magnetic-field component along increasing toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, with R the major radius and Z the vertical height. It equals +1 for a component directed toward increasing toroidal angle and -1 for the opposite direction, and is undefined when B_phi vanishes. Unit: 1.
record.documentation:
The toroidal magnetic-field sign specifies whether the equilibrium toroidal field component on a flux surface is directed along or opposite increasing toroidal angle in local gyrokinetic geometry.

For a nonzero toroidal magnetic-field component, the orientation indicator is defined by

$$
s_\phi = \operatorname{sgn}(B_\phi) = \frac{B_\phi}{|B_\phi|}
$$

where $s_\phi$ is the orientation indicator, $B_\phi$ is the toroidal magnetic-field component, and $\operatorname{sgn}$ is the sign function. The component is $B_\phi = \mathbf{B}\cdot\hat{\phi}$, where $\mathbf{B}$ is the equilibrium magnetic field and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector toward increasing toroidal angle. The right-handed cylindrical frame is $(R,\phi,Z)$, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

As the toroidal member of [parity](name:parity), this quantity retains only field orientation and takes the values $+1$ or $-1$; the two-valued indicator is undefined when the toroidal component vanishes. It does not specify field strength, plasma-current direction, or the even or odd symmetry of a gyrokinetic perturbation.

Sign convention: Positive when the toroidal magnetic-field component points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.
record.name: parity_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_at_flux_surface

reason: The source specifies “Resistivity of the mobile unit,” within “Set of mobile units” and “In case of mobile plasma facing components”. These words identify the locus as a mobile plasma-facing component unit, rather than a plasma-facing component without that qualification.

record.description: Electrical resistivity of the material assigned to a mobile plasma-facing component unit, relating local electric field to current density and governing its conductive electromagnetic response.
record.documentation:
Electrical resistivity is the material property that determines the electric field required to sustain conduction in a mobile plasma-facing component unit. It governs induced-current and eddy-current response within that unit.

For an isotropic material, the local constitutive relation is

$$
\mathbf{E} = \rho\,\mathbf{J}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}$ is the local electric-field vector, $\rho$ is the electrical resistivity, and $\mathbf{J}$ is the conventional current-density vector.

This quantity applies to the material of one mobile plasma-facing component unit and is not summed over multiple units or converted into a lumped resistance. It is a local material property, distinct from the effective resistivity of a broader passive conducting structure or [wall material](name:resistivity_of_wall_material). When geometry is included, it contributes to a lumped [passive-loop resistance](name:resistance_of_passive_loop), which also depends on current-path length and cross-sectional geometry.
record.name: resistivity_of_mobile_plasma_facing_component_unit

reason: The case states, "Gas-particle count and equivalent-electron count use different counting bases." Adding the required equivalent_electron qualifier yields the existing neighbour "accumulated_total_prefill_gas_equivalent_electron_count", defined as "the cumulative gas amount injected before plasma breakdown, summed over all atomic and molecular species as an equivalent-electron count." The corrected name therefore collides with an existing record for the same quantity.

record.description: Cumulative equivalent-electron inventory of all gas species introduced by injection during the plasma prefill phase, summed over species.
record.documentation:
This quantity is the total gas inventory accumulated during the plasma prefill phase, expressed as an equivalent-electron count and summed over all injected species. It represents the integrated amount introduced before plasma breakdown, rather than an instantaneous injection rate.

The accumulated equivalent-electron count is defined by

$$
N_{\mathrm{eq}}(t) = \sum_s \int_{t_0}^{\min(t,t_1)} \dot{N}_{s,\mathrm{eq}}(t')\,dt'
$$

where $s$ indexes injected gas species, $\dot{N}_{s,\mathrm{eq}}$ is the equivalent-electron injection rate of species $s$, $t_0$ and $t_1$ delimit the prefill phase, and $t$ is the evaluation time. The sum includes all species; a species-specific quantity such as [accumulated hydrogen prefill count](name:accumulated_hydrogen_prefill_count) is a component of this total. The quantity is distinct from the instantaneous injection rate and from inventories restricted to one species, while [accumulated prefill gas count](name:accumulated_prefill_gas_count) denotes the near-equivalent total inventory.
record.name: accumulated_total_prefill_gas_count

reason: The source specifies “Processed image in apparent temperature,” contradicting the incumbent's “thermodynamic temperature” and “surface material state.” The source also states “ndim=2,” “First dimension : row index (horizontal orientation). Second dimension: column index (vertical orientation)” and “The size of this matrix is assumed to be constant over time.” The available qualifier “radiative” distinguishes this infrared-radiance-derived quantity from thermodynamic surface temperature.

record.description: Radiative surface temperature is the apparent temperature assigned from infrared radiation to the exposed material boundary of a plasma-facing component at a specified surface point and time, expressed in K. It refers to the apparent surface temperature, not to an area aggregate or regional extremum. The processed image is a two-dimensional matrix whose first dimension is the row index (horizontal orientation) and whose second dimension is the column index (vertical orientation); the size of this matrix is assumed to be constant over time.
record.documentation: Radiative surface temperature is the apparent temperature assigned from infrared radiation to the material at the exposed boundary of a plasma-facing component. It is a local scalar assigned to a specified material surface point and time, representing the apparent temperature inferred from infrared radiance rather than necessarily the thermodynamic state of the surface material. For an extended exposed surface, the unqualified quantity denotes the local point value at each surface point, not an area average, integral, percentile, or extremum. Region-level aggregates require distinct standard names; the maximum over a specified exposed surface region is [maximum_surface_temperature](name:maximum_surface_temperature). [temperature_at_wall](name:temperature_at_wall) is the thermodynamic boundary-locus temperature when the wall is the defining locus.
record.name: radiative_surface_temperature

reason: The definition omits the source requirements “Phase measured for this wavelength, corrected from fringe jumps”, “for each frequency and time slice (corresponding to the begin time of a sweep), relative to the phase at launch”, and “Phase of the envelope of the probing signal, relative to the phase at launch”, together with the stated “ndim=0” and “ndim=1” dimensionalities. These details belong in the definition; they do not require adding correction methods or phase-reference conventions to the name.

record.description: Wave phase of the wave beam is the angular argument of the probing-wave envelope; when referenced to launch, it is the envelope phase offset from the launch phase. The value is expressed in radians. For interferometry, it is measured for the specified wavelength and corrected from fringe jumps, with zero non-time array dimensions. For fluctuation reflectometry, it is measured for each frequency and time slice, corresponding to the begin time of a sweep, relative to the phase at launch, with zero non-time array dimensions. For refractometry, it is the envelope phase of the probing signal in the specified channel and frequency bandwidth, relative to the phase at launch, with one non-time array dimension whose coordinate is not specified. Launch-referenced phase is the envelope phase minus the launch phase, using the same phase convention; positive phase advances counterclockwise under the positive-time-exponent phasor convention. Phase is equivalent modulo 2π, while fringe-jump correction changes its unwrapped representation.
record.documentation:
The wave phase is the angular argument of the complex probing-wave envelope at the wave-beam locus. It is defined relative to a phase origin; when the origin is the launch phase, the value is a signed phase difference rather than an absolute phase with a universal zero.

For a launch-referenced value, the phase difference is:

$$
\varphi = \varphi_{\mathrm{env}} - \varphi_{\mathrm{launch}} \pmod{2\pi}
$$

where $\varphi$ is the launch-referenced phase difference, represented by difference of wave phase and launched wave phase of the wave beam; $\varphi_{\mathrm{env}}$ is the envelope phase at the wave-beam locus; and $\varphi_{\mathrm{launch}}$ is the launched wave phase. The phases use the same phase convention, and $2\pi$ is one full phase revolution.

This quantity is the envelope phase, not the carrier oscillation phase. Values differing by an integer number of full revolutions represent the same phase; an unwrapped phase selects a continuous branch, and fringe-jump correction changes that representation without changing the phase modulo one revolution.

Sign convention: Positive when the envelope phase at the wave-beam locus advances counterclockwise relative to the launch phase, using the positive-time-exponent phasor convention.
record.name: wave_phase_of_wave_beam

record.description: Net conventional electric current carried by charged particles into all divertor target surfaces, including signed electron and ion contributions.
record.documentation:
The total divertor current is the algebraic conventional current delivered by charged particles crossing the plasma-facing surfaces of the complete divertor assembly. It includes ion and electron contributions and excludes neutral-particle flux and displacement current.

The current is defined by

$$
I_{\mathrm{div}} = \int_{S_{\mathrm{div}}} \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{ch}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}\, dA = \int_{S_{\mathrm{div}}} \sum_s q_s\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_s \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}\, dA
$$

where $I_{\mathrm{div}}$ is the total current in A, $S_{\mathrm{div}}$ is the union of divertor target surfaces, $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{ch}}$ is conventional charged-particle current density in A m$^{-2}$, $q_s$ is the signed charge of species $s$ in C, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_s$ is its particle flux density in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ points from the plasma toward the material.

This assembly-integrated quantity differs from [current at a divertor target](name:current_at_divertor_target), which applies to one target, and [current of a divertor tile](name:current_of_divertor_tile), which applies to an individual tile.

Sign convention: Positive when conventional charged-particle current flows from the plasma into the divertor material.
record.name: current_of_divertor
